# Methods

Let $N_{it}$ be the number of claims in tract $i$ and year $t$, $e_{it}$ the exposure in policy-years, and $\mathbf{x}_{it}$ the vector of features built from policy information known at inception. All three models predict the expected count $\mu_{it}$ with $\log e_{it}$ as an offset, so they share the same target and the same exposure adjustment.

**[TO FILL BY TEAM: confirm that the three models use the same feature set]**

## Poisson GLM

$$
N_{it}\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_{it}),\qquad \log\mu_{it}=\log e_{it}+\mathbf{x}_{it}^\top\boldsymbol\beta
$$ {#eq-poisson}

The Poisson GLM is the reference model for claim counts. The log link makes the effects multiplicative, and the offset turns the model into a model of the claim rate per policy-year, so tracts with different exposure are directly comparable. It assumes that the variance equals the mean, which the next model relaxes.

## Negative Binomial GLM

$$
\text{Var}(N_{it})=\mu_{it}+\alpha\mu_{it}^2
$$ {#eq-nb}

The negative binomial GLM keeps the mean structure of @eq-poisson and adds a dispersion parameter $\alpha$. Flood claims cluster in event years, so counts are likely to vary more than a Poisson model allows. The Poisson model is the limit $\alpha \to 0$, so the comparison shows whether modelling overdispersion changes the predictions or only their uncertainty.

**[TO FILL BY TEAM: estimation method for $\alpha$]**

## LightGBM with Poisson Objective

LightGBM fits gradient boosted trees by minimizing the Poisson negative log-likelihood, with $\log e_{it}$ as initial score. The initial score plays the role of the offset, so the trees learn the log claim rate relative to exposure, as in the GLMs. Unlike the GLMs, the trees can capture non-linear effects and interactions without specifying them in advance, which is the flexibility that RQ1 evaluates.

## Validation

Hyperparameters and model choices are selected by forward-chaining validation inside 2010 to 2019: each fold trains on earlier years and validates on the following year. This respects the time order and mimics the real task of predicting future years without using future information. The test years 2020 to 2024 are used only once, for the final evaluation, and never for tuning.

## Metrics

All metrics are fixed in advance, before looking at the test years.

- **Poisson deviance** on the test years:
  $$
  D=2\sum_{i,t}\left[y_{it}\log\frac{y_{it}}{\hat\mu_{it}}-(y_{it}-\hat\mu_{it})\right],
  $$ {#eq-deviance}
  with $y_{it}\log(y_{it}/\hat\mu_{it})=0$ when $y_{it}=0$. It is the natural loss for count predictions and the quantity the Poisson models optimize, so it compares the three models on a common scale. Lower is better.
- **Calibration by prediction decile.** Test tract-years are grouped into ten classes of predicted frequency, and predicted and observed claims are compared in each class. This shows whether a model is biased for low-risk or high-risk tracts, which the deviance alone does not reveal.
- **Gini index.** It measures how well a model ranks tract-years from low to high risk, independently of the level of the predictions. Ranking is what matters for risk segmentation. **[TO FILL BY TEAM: exact Gini definition (exposure-weighted or not)]**
- **Predicted versus observed totals per test year.** This checks aggregate bias year by year, which matters because the test window contains Hurricane Ian (2022) and Hurricane Helene (2024).

Results are reported overall and for Florida versus the other seven states, because Florida accounts for about 71% of policy records and 57% of claims and could dominate the overall metrics.

**Sensitivity check.** The models are refitted with a target that counts all claims, not only claims with a positive paid amount, to check whether the comparison depends on the claim definition.
